recall.a: He named unsettled ties with the US, shocks in energy markets, and India's lack of an AI play. Countries are being pushed to pick a side, but India's size and location mean it cannot. So it must hedge, even though hedging costs much more.

cards.title: India cuts its bond borrowing plan by ₹1.2 trillion
cards.body: India's government will borrow ₹1.2 trillion less through bonds this financial year (FY27) than the Budget planned. Money is coming in faster than expected. But the deficit target has not changed.

sections.text:
The finance ministry and the RBI announced the new plan on Friday. Economists say income is stronger than expected. Tax receipts are higher, and selling government stakes in companies brought in more money. From April to July, non-tax revenue had already reached 63.5% of its full-year estimate.

One detail matters. A finance ministry official says net borrowing stays at the Budget level. Net borrowing is the part that pays for the deficit (the gap between spending and income). So the Budget's deficit plan holds. The government is not promising a smaller deficit.

sections.label: The numbers
sections.text:
₹15.995 trillion: the new FY27 plan for dated securities (bonds that pay back on a fixed date), down from ₹17.2 trillion
₹7.86 trillion: to be raised from October to March, over 23 weekly auctions
26.8%: share of the full-year deficit target used by July, against 29.9% a year earlier
4.3% of GDP: the Budget's deficit target for FY27

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Fewer new bonds means less debt for the market to absorb. That could calm bond yields (the interest rate the market asks), which have been rising. PwC's Ranen Banerjee says it may also let the RBI's rate committee wait for more data before raising rates. But yields also depend on inflation, RBI policy, cash in the banking system and investor demand.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: The government is leaning more on long bonds. They make up 26.46% of second-half issuance, up from 23% in the first half. The official says this means less debt falls due at once. But Emkay's Madhavi Arora warns it is a lot of long-term supply for the market to absorb, while global rates offer little comfort.

recall.q: Why did the government cut its bond borrowing plan, and why doesn't that mean a smaller deficit?
recall.a: Money is coming in faster: higher tax receipts, strong non-tax revenue and stake sales. But net borrowing, the part that pays for the deficit, stays at the Budget level. So the deficit plan is unchanged.

cards.title: Clean power priced below new coal in India's auction
cards.body: In an Indian auction, clean power backed by batteries won at ₹5.25 per unit, fixed for 25 years. Sellers must supply power the way a coal plant does, day and night. New coal starts higher, at about ₹5.8, and its price keeps rising.

sections.text:
A "unit" is one kilowatt-hour, the unit on your power bill.

The Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI), a government power buyer, ran the auction for 1,000 MW. Sellers must pair renewable power with batteries. Like a coal plant, they must send most power in the evening, at night and early in the morning, and less at midday, when solar is plentiful. Output is checked every 15 minutes. If a seller falls short, it pays 1.5 times the contract price.

Coal's price does not stay fixed. India signed seven new coal contracts in 2025. They started at ₹5.4 to ₹6.3 per unit, about ₹5.8 on average. These prices rise as fuel costs go up. The authors estimate they could average ₹7.4 by 2050. The ₹5.25 price never rises. With 4% yearly inflation, it is like paying about ₹3.79 in today's money.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 16 bidders, 7 winners, and every winning bid at ₹5.25–5.26
NTPC's green arm bid just 3% above the winning price, and ReNew less than 1% above
₹350–1,300 crore: estimated yearly saving from this 1 GW compared with new coal

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Planners keep building coal because they believe only coal gives reliable power around the clock. This auction tested that belief with real, binding bids. The bids were very close together, so the price is not one reckless bidder's gamble. A fixed price also protects buyers if fuel and transport costs go up.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: One auction proves a price, not performance. The projects must be built in less than two years. For now, the claim that they can last through monsoons and cloudy weeks comes only from models by the authors' own team. The contract also does not demand full output every hour: 90% in six hours the buyer picks, 70% in other non-solar hours, and 50–60% at midday. CSEP, a policy research group, estimates ₹8.3–11.8 per unit if full output were required every hour. The authors reply that the 15-minute checks answer much of that concern.

recall.q: Clean power with batteries won India's auction at ₹5.25 per unit. Why does it beat coal by more than the starting prices suggest, and what does the auction not yet prove?
recall.a: New coal starts at about ₹5.8 and keeps rising as fuel costs go up, perhaps to ₹7.4 by 2050. The ₹5.25 price is fixed for 25 years, so inflation makes it cheaper in real terms every year. But this is one 1,000 MW auction for projects not yet built, and their reliability comes from models, not real operation.

cards.title: Friends help the aging brain, but not against stress
cards.body: In a study of nearly 3,900 adults over 50, people with more social support lost less attention as they aged. But support did not soften the harm of long-running stress. Friends helped the mind, but they were not a shield.

sections.text:
Money trouble that never ends. Heavy demands at work. Fights with people close to you. Caring for someone who is sick. Your own health problems. Researchers call this chronic stress: stress that stays for a long time, not the quick kind that comes and goes.

A team at Wake Forest University School of Medicine asked 3,873 adults aged 50 and older about these stressors. They also asked how much support people felt they got from family, friends and community. The average age was 64.8. No one had dementia at the start. Most (78%) had normal thinking. The other 22% had mild cognitive impairment, which means early, mild thinking problems.

Every two years, people took tests of four mental skills: attention, episodic memory (remembering events), language, and executive function (planning and controlling your thinking). The team tracked how each skill changed over time.

First, the good news. People with more social support at the start lost less attention over the years. This was true for men and women, and across racial and ethnic groups.

Now the surprise. Many people hope friends work like a cushion that softens stress. Scientists call this a buffer. Here, support did not work as a buffer. High stress was linked to decline in thinking in the same way, whether people had a lot of support or very little.

Stress also did not hit everyone the same way. Women with high stress lost more attention and language skill than men. Hispanic participants with high stress lost more memory than non-Hispanic White participants.

The lesson is clear. Being social cannot replace dealing with stress directly. Protecting the aging mind probably needs two things together: help that reduces the stressors themselves, and community efforts that keep people connected. The lead researcher, Michelle Mielke, points out that both stress and social ties may be possible to change. Next, the team wants to learn how stress reaches the brain. They will look at the body's stress-hormone system (the HPA axis), long-term inflammation, and damage to tiny blood vessels.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This was an observational study. It shows links, not causes. People reported their own stress and support, and these were measured only once, at the start. The article does not say how big the differences between groups were. And no one has yet tested whether programs that cut stress or build support would actually protect thinking.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Friends can steady the aging mind, but they cannot carry its stress away. The stress itself has to shrink.

recall.q: In this study, what did social support help with, what did it fail to do, and what does that mean?
recall.a: More support went with less loss of attention, in every group. But it did not soften stress: high stress was linked to decline just as much with strong support as with weak support. So stress has to be reduced directly. Friends cannot replace that.
